beginner: Deep soil that drains well is best, ideally a sandy loam or loam.
seasoned: Deep, well-drained sandy loam to loam, slightly acidic
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Sandy or rocky soil is fine if you water and feed enough. Heavy soil works only if you plant on a raised mound so water drains away.
seasoned: Sandy and rocky soils with adequate water and feeding; heavy soils only on a raised mound or berm that guarantees drainage
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Avoid heavy clay that drains poorly and any spot where water pools. Wet roots lead to a root rot that kills citrus.
seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay and any low spot where water stands, which invites Phytophthora foot and root rot
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Mandarins care most about drainage. They want deep soil that drains well and stays slightly acidic, kept evenly moist but never soggy. If water sits around the roots, the tree can get a root rot that is the most common way citrus dies. Heavy clay holds water, so the fix is to build a low mound and set the tree on top so the crown drains. Keep the knobby graft union above the soil. If your soil is alkaline (high pH), common in the desert and inland West, the tree may run short on iron and zinc, so feed a citrus fertilizer that includes them.
seasoned: Mandarins share the citrus non-negotiable: sharp drainage. They do best in deep, well-drained sandy loam to loam, slightly acidic, with steady moisture and no waterlogging. Saturated roots invite Phytophthora foot and root rot, one of the most serious threats to a citrus tree. On heavy ground plant high on a raised mound or berm so the root crown drains freely, and keep the graft union clear of the soil line. On high-pH alkaline soils, common in desert and interior-West regions, iron and zinc lock up and the tree shows chlorosis, so use a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer and acidify slowly with elemental sulfur.

beginner: Mandarins like soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. The main thing to watch is alkaline (high pH) soil, common in the desert and inland West, where the tree cannot take up iron and zinc and the leaves yellow while the veins stay green. If that happens, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc, and over time add sulfur to make the soil a little more acidic.
seasoned: Mandarins prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerate a somewhat wider band. The practical problem is high-pH alkaline soil (common in the desert Southwest and interior West), where iron and zinc become chemically unavailable and the tree shows interveinal chlorosis even though the nutrients are present. Correct with chelated micronutrients and a citrus fertilizer that supplies them, and acidify gradually with elemental sulfur for a durable fix.

beginner: Mandarins are hungry for nitrogen and want most of their food during the growing season. Start feeding a grown tree as the weather warms in late winter or early spring, keep it up through summer in a few split doses, then stop by late summer so the new growth toughens before cool weather. A mandarin is a smaller tree than an orange, so it needs less total feed. Feed young trees smaller amounts more often. If your soil is alkaline, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow, and do not overfeed, since soft growth draws pests.
seasoned: Mandarins are nitrogen-hungry like all citrus and feed best on a rhythm concentrated in the growing season. Feed a bearing tree from late winter or early spring through summer in split applications, and stop by late summer so the fall flush hardens before winter cold. Because mandarins are smaller trees than a navel orange, scale the total nitrogen down accordingly. Young trees get smaller, more frequent doses to build the framework. On alkaline soils use a citrus fertilizer that supplies iron, zinc, and manganese as chelates and water it in. Over-fertilizing pushes soft flush that draws aphids, leafminer, and psyllid.

beginner: A fertilizer made for citrus (look for one labeled citrus); these are higher in nitrogen and include the iron and zinc citrus needs
seasoned: A nitrogen-forward citrus formulation (for example a 2-1-1 ratio) with included micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese), or a product labeled specifically for citrus

beginner: Give more as the tree gets bigger, following the amounts on the citrus fertilizer label and splitting it across spring and summer. A small young tree needs only a little; a grown mandarin needs more, though still less than a full-size orange tree. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.
seasoned: Scale nitrogen to tree age and size, and note that a mandarin's smaller canopy needs less than a full-size orange. Follow the citrus product label and local extension rates, which vary by region and soil, and divide the year's nitrogen across spring-to-summer applications, with proportionally less for young trees.

beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under a mandarin tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, beats grass growing right up to the tree. There is little real benefit to planting things close around citrus.
seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes hard for water and nutrients in the shallow layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and mowers damage the trunk. A mulched, grass-free basin out to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus, mandarins included. Low, shallow-rooted covers or a cool-season legume kept outside the trunk flare add living mulch without root competition. Mandarins fruit on a single tree, so no pollinizer companion is required; in fact nearby pollen-bearing citrus can put seeds into otherwise seedless fruit.

beginner.name: White clover
beginner.why_beginner: A low clover outside the trunk area works as a living mulch and adds a little nitrogen, without stealing water the way lawn grass does.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume living-mulch / cover crop under citrus is extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen transfer is site-dependent and clover also competes for water.

beginner.name: Marigold
beginner.why_beginner: A simple flower that brings in helpful insects and fills bare ground around the tree. Plant it beyond the trunk, not tight against it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Marigold beneficial-insect draw and root-knot nematode suppression are partly grounded as general mechanisms; applied to citrus by analogy, no mandarin-specific trial located.

seasoned.name: Fava bean
seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season nitrogen fixer grown beyond the dripline as a winter cover, then cut and dropped to feed the soil without crowding the tree.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Cool-season legume cover crops in citrus are extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen-transfer magnitude is site and timing dependent.

beginner: Yarrow is a low, tough plant with flat flower heads that pull in ladybugs, lacewings, and other good bugs that eat aphids. It is shallow-rooted and easygoing, so it does not crowd the tree as long as you keep it out toward the edge of the canopy. Let it flower to get the benefit.
seasoned: A low, shallow-rooted plant that draws beneficial insects and does not compete with citrus roots when kept outside the dripline.

beginner: St. Augustine is a thick, fast-spreading lawn grass that is rough on citrus. It soaks up water and food in the top layer of soil where the tree's roots feed, and it creeps to the trunk. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base and hold the grass back beyond it.
seasoned: A dense, spreading lawn grass that competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the topsoil and creeps right up to the trunk. Keep it cleared out to the dripline.

beginner: This tiny brown insect rests on new leaves at an angle, rear end raised, which is your clue. The young ones make little waxy white threads and curl the new leaf tips. The real danger is not the feeding but a fatal disease it spreads, citrus greening, so it is worth acting on even where the pest is uncommon.
seasoned: A tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Nymphs make waxy tubules and curl tender growth. The insect matters less for its feeding than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide. Scout the youngest flush.

beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is pushing tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and build fastest in warm weather when the tree pushes tender growth. The pest is established across much of the southern United States, and any psyllid should be treated as a potential disease carrier.

beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone, since that is how the pest and its disease spread. Check new leaves often in warm weather, and follow local guidance if greening is in your area.
seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area, the main way the pest and disease jump regions. Inspect each flush in the warm season, and conserve the parasitic wasp Tamarixia and general predators that suppress it.

beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, repeating each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is above about 95°F or the tree is short on water, or the oil can burn leaves. Also report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor.
seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap on the new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage is key, repeated as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most important, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.

beginner: You will see squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled. A tiny caterpillar makes these tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts a grown tree, though it can set back a small young one.
seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark frass line down each mine and leaf margins that curl around the damage. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage; hardened leaves are not attacked. On an established tree the injury is cosmetic, but on a young mandarin pushing lots of flush it can slow growth.

beginner: A tiny moth lays eggs on the newest leaves, and the larvae tunnel inside them. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows on the late-summer growth.
seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush, and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on the late-summer and fall flushes rather than spring growth.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize or prune a lot in summer, because that creates the tender leaves the moth needs. On a healthy grown tree it is best to live with the trails, since helpful wasps keep it in check.
seasoned: Avoid forcing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen or unnecessary summer pruning, since the moth needs young leaves to breed. Tolerate cosmetic mining on bearing trees; resident parasitic wasps usually provide good control when broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.

beginner: Usually no treatment is needed, and spraying can kill the good bugs that control it. On a small young tree you want to protect, light horticultural oil on the new leaves discourages the moth. Only spray in mild conditions, not in high heat or on a thirsty tree, and leave the tunneled leaves on.
seasoned: Chemical control is rarely warranted, and broad-spectrum sprays undermine the parasitic wasps. On a young tree where mining slows establishment, a light horticultural oil at bud break discourages egg-laying on the new flush; repeat as each flush emerges. Follow label heat limits and do not spray above 95°F. Leave mined leaves in place.

beginner: Scale look like little hard or waxy lumps that sit still on twigs and leaf undersides, so it is easy to mistake them for part of the branch. The soft kinds make leaves sticky and grow a black sooty coating, and ants are often crawling around them.
seasoned: Fixed, non-moving bumps clustered on twigs, along the leaf midrib, and beneath leaves. Armored types form firm gray or brown shells like raised bark; softer types are plumper and glossy and secrete honeydew that leaves foliage tacky and grows black sooty mold, with ants patrolling for the sugar. Heavy numbers bring mottled yellow leaves, early leaf fall, and twig dieback.

beginner: Scale are little insects that feed on the tree's sap. They get worst when ants are around, since the ants protect them from the helpful bugs that eat scale.
seasoned: A mix of armored and soft scale species tap into the tree and feed on sap. They gain the upper hand on trees that are dusty, crowded, or patrolled by ants, since ants drive off the ladybugs and parasitic wasps that would thin the colony.

beginner: Keep ants from climbing the tree with a sticky band around the trunk, which lets the good bugs control the scale, and look over any new tree for lumps before planting it.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, rinse dust off the canopy, and cut off ants with a sticky trunk band so resident beneficials can work. Inspect any incoming nursery tree, since scale often hitchhikes on new stock.

beginner: Coat the lumps with horticultural oil, reaching the backs of leaves and the twigs. Save the spray for cooler, well-watered days, never above roughly 95°F or on a stressed tree, or it can scorch the foliage. Spray again later as new ones appear.
seasoned: A thorough horticultural oil application, narrow-range petroleum or neem, smothers scale; the key is wetting every surface, especially twig undersides and leaf backs. Skip oil above roughly 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree. Plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.

beginner: Look for clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, often green or black, packed onto the newest leaves and flower buds, curling the tips. They leave a sticky coating that ants follow and that grows a black sooty film. Mandarins are most vulnerable during the spring and fall flushes.
seasoned: Clusters of soft green, black, or brown aphids on the youngest flush and flower buds, with curled, distorted new leaves and sticky honeydew that draws ants and grows sooty mold. Spring and fall flushes are the targets. The brown citrus aphid is also a vector of citrus tristeza virus, which raises the stakes where that disease is a concern.

beginner: Aphids multiply very fast on soft new growth in mild weather, and ants protect them. Too much fertilizer makes extra tender leaves that draw them in.
seasoned: Aphids reproduce explosively on tender new growth in mild weather and are tended by ants for honeydew. Lush, over-fertilized flush is especially attractive, and ant protection lets colonies outrun their natural enemies.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize, which makes the soft growth aphids love, and keep ants out so ladybugs and other helpers can eat them. A blast of water from the hose usually clears them off.
seasoned: Avoid forcing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Control ants so ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps can suppress colonies. A strong jet of water knocks aphids off new growth and is often all that is needed.

beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, getting under the curled leaves. Keep oil for mild days only, not in high heat or on a stressed tree, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.
seasoned: A forceful water spray, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil controls aphids; cover the undersides of curled leaves and repeat as needed. Observe oil heat limits (not above 95°F or on stressed trees), and preserve natural enemies by skipping broad-spectrum insecticides.

beginner: Look for leaves that turn a dull, speckled, silvery color, sometimes with tiny red dots moving on them (a hand lens helps). Mites get worse when it is hot, dry, and dusty. A lot of them can bronze the leaves and drop some.
seasoned: Fine stippling or silvering on leaves and sometimes the rind, with tiny dark-red mites and cast skins visible under a hand lens. Heavy populations bronze the foliage and can drop leaves. Mites flare in hot, dusty, dry conditions and after broad-spectrum sprays remove their predators, so an outbreak often signals a dust-stressed or over-sprayed tree.

beginner: These mites love hot, dusty conditions and build up fast on stressed trees. Dusty trees and trees sprayed with strong insecticides (which kill the helpful mites) get the worst of it.
seasoned: Citrus red mite thrives in heat and dust and reproduces rapidly on stressed trees. Dusty roadside trees and trees sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides, which remove predatory mites, are the most prone to damaging populations.

beginner: Rinse dust off the leaves during hot, dry weather and keep the tree watered, because a healthy tree handles mites better. Avoid strong insecticides that kill the good mites.
seasoned: Hose dust off the canopy in hot, dry spells and keep the tree well watered, since vigorous trees tolerate mites better. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that destroy the predatory mites providing natural control.

beginner: Usually the damage is just cosmetic and needs nothing. If there are a lot of mites, horticultural oil works, but timing is tricky: mites peak in hot weather, the riskiest time to oil a tree. Only spray once it has cooled off, never on a hot, dry, stressed tree.
seasoned: Damage is usually cosmetic and rarely needs treatment. If populations run heavy on a stressed tree, horticultural oil provides control; observe heat limits strictly, as mite outbreaks coincide with the hot weather when oil is riskiest. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree.

beginner: The classic sign is a leaf yellow in a blotchy, uneven pattern, with the yellow on one side not matching the other (a nutrient problem is usually even on both sides). Fruit stay small, lopsided, green on the bottom, and taste bad. There is no cure, and the tree slowly dies. It is the worst citrus disease there is.
seasoned: Blotchy, asymmetric leaf yellowing that does not mirror across the midrib (distinguishing it from a symmetric nutrient deficiency), yellow shoots, and corky, enlarged veins. Fruit are small, lopsided, fail to color fully, stay green at the bottom, and taste bitter and salty; seeds often abort. The tree declines over years and there is no cure. This is the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.

beginner: Bacteria spread by the Asian citrus psyllid as it feeds on new shoots clog the tree's plumbing, blocking food to roots and fruit. No treatment reverses it; an affected tree is a permanent source of spread. Management is preventing psyllid feeding and removing any confirmed tree.
seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, the bacterium behind greening, spreads tree to tree by the Asian citrus psyllid feeding on new growth, then clogs the phloem so nutrients cannot reach roots and fruit. No treatment clears an established infection, so management is entirely suppressing the psyllid and removing confirmed trees before they seed further spread.

beginner: Buy only certified clean trees, never move citrus out of a quarantine zone, and control the psyllid that spreads it. Check your tree often, and report anything that looks like greening to your local agricultural office, because removing infected trees quickly protects everyone's citrus.
seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees, never move citrus out of quarantine areas, and control the psyllid aggressively where it is present. Inspect regularly and report suspected greening to your county agricultural commissioner, since coordinated removal of infected trees is the only effective area-wide defense.

beginner: There is no treatment that saves an infected tree. Focus entirely on prevention: keep the psyllid off with regular inspection and treatment, and if a tree is diagnosed with greening, remove it promptly to protect nearby trees. An infected tree left in place becomes an ongoing source of psyllid pressure.
seasoned: There is no cure and no organic remedy for an infected tree. Management is prevention and vector control only: protect trees from the psyllid, and remove and properly dispose of confirmed-infected trees promptly so they cannot serve as a reservoir.

beginner: Look for gum oozing near the base of the trunk and a dark, sunken, slimy patch under the bark, along with a thinning, yellowing canopy. A key clue is leaves that wilt and do not perk up when you water, because the roots are rotting from too much water.
seasoned: A trunk lesion at or near the bud union, appearing first as a drop of gum, then a brown, necrotic, slippery area under the bark that can girdle the trunk. Below ground, dark, rotted feeder roots go with a thinning, yellowing canopy and leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering. It is one of the most serious threats to a citrus tree, and it follows wet feet and a buried graft union.

beginner: A soil fungus attacks the roots and trunk base when the soil stays too wet. Poor drainage, overwatering, and burying the graft knob are what let it in.
seasoned: Soil-borne Phytophthora species attack roots and the crown wherever soil stays saturated. A buried or mulch-packed graft union, poor drainage, and overwatering are the drivers; heavy clay and standing water are the classic setups.

beginner: Plant on a raised mound with the graft knob above the soil, make sure water drains fast, keep mulch off the trunk, and let the soil dry between waterings. Buying a tree on a root-rot-resistant rootstock also helps a lot.
seasoned: Plant high on a mound with the graft union well clear of the soil, guarantee sharp drainage, keep mulch off the trunk, and water with a soak-and-dry rhythm rather than constant moisture. Choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock, which most trifoliate and citrumelo stocks provide.

beginner: There is no easy fix once it takes hold. Improve the drainage, clear soil and mulch away from the trunk base so it can dry out, and water less. The best control is preventing it with good drainage and planting the tree high in the first place.
seasoned: There is no quick cure once the crown is girdled. Correct the cause: improve drainage, pull soil and mulch back from the crown to let it dry, and cut back irrigation. Minor bark lesions can sometimes be exposed and allowed to callus. Prevention through drainage and planting depth is the real control.

beginner: Small brown or black spots with a yellow ring show up on young leaves and shoot tips, and dark, slightly sunken spots appear on small fruit, which may then drop. This one mainly troubles certain tangerine-type mandarins and tangelos (like Minneola and Murcott); satsuma and clementine are not among the types UF lists as susceptible.
seasoned: Small brown-to-black necrotic spots, often ringed by a yellow halo, on young leaves and shoot tips, plus small, slightly depressed dark spots on young fruit that can cause premature drop. It is a mandarin-and-tangerine-hybrid disease: Dancy tangerine and Minneola tangelo are most severely affected, with Murcott, Orlando, Lee, Nova, and Sunburst often hit. Fruit becomes more resistant as it matures, so mostly young fruit is affected.

beginner: A fungus infects the young leaves and small fruit of susceptible mandarin hybrids, spreading in warm, wet, humid weather. It cannot infect older leaves or older fruit.
seasoned: The tangerine pathotype of the fungus Alternaria alternata infects only young, susceptible tissue and spreads on warm, wet, humid weather, so it is most damaging in the humid Southeast and on the susceptible hybrid cultivars. Older, hardened leaves and older fruit are not infected.

beginner: The easiest fix is picking the right variety: satsuma and clementine are not among the susceptible types, so choose those in humid areas instead of a susceptible one like Minneola. Otherwise, prune for good airflow, avoid wetting the leaves, and rake up fallen leaves.
seasoned: The strongest control is variety choice: satsuma and clementine are not among the varieties UF lists as susceptible, so plant those in humid regions rather than a highly susceptible hybrid like Minneola or Murcott. Prune for airflow, avoid overhead wetting, and clear fallen leaves. Copper fungicides on the susceptible flush are the fallback where a prized susceptible variety is grown.

beginner: If you grow a susceptible type, copper sprays on the new growth during warm, wet weather help protect it, following the label. Spots already there will not heal. On satsuma or clementine you generally do not need to spray at all.
seasoned: On a susceptible cultivar, time copper fungicide applications to protect the new flush and small fruit during warm, wet spells, following label rates; there is no rescue for tissue already spotted. On a tolerant variety no treatment is needed.

beginner: Yellow blotches on top of the leaf with a greasy-looking brown or black blister underneath, followed by leaves dropping, mostly in winter and early spring. It shows up mainly in warm, humid places like Florida and the Gulf Coast.
seasoned: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface with a matching blister-like swelling underneath that collapses into a brown-to-black, greasy-looking spot. Infected leaves drop, mostly in winter and early spring, thinning the canopy. It is a warm, humid-climate disease, most troublesome in Florida and the Gulf where relative humidity is high.

beginner: A fungus infects the undersides of the leaves in warm, humid weather, and it builds up on old fallen leaves under the tree. It is mainly a problem in humid climates, not dry ones.
seasoned: A fungus infects the underside of leaves during warm, humid, wet weather, with spores building on decaying fallen leaves on the ground. High relative humidity and warm nights are what drive it, so it is a Southeastern and Gulf concern rather than an arid-West one.

beginner: Rake up and remove the fallen leaves under the tree, since that is where the fungus builds, and keep the canopy open for airflow. In humid areas a summer oil or copper spray helps if it is bad.
seasoned: Rake up and remove fallen leaves to cut the spore source, prune for airflow, and keep the tree vigorous. A summer horticultural-oil or copper application, timed to the main infection period, reduces it where pressure is high.

beginner: A summer spray of horticultural oil (with copper if needed) controls it on a backyard tree, along with cleaning up fallen leaves. In dry climates you usually do not need to do anything.
seasoned: Horticultural oil, alone or with copper, applied in early to mid-summer gives good backyard control by smothering the developing infection; sanitation of fallen leaves supports it. In arid regions it rarely warrants treatment.

beginner: Once picked, mandarins last about a week on the counter, a bit less than an orange because the skin is so thin. They are best eaten fresh and soon.
seasoned: Picked mandarins keep about one week at room temperature, less than a thick-skinned orange because the loose, thin rind offers little protection. Use them fresh; the whole appeal of a mandarin is eating it soon after picking.

beginner: In the fridge, mandarins last two to four weeks. Keep them loose or in a bag with holes so they do not get damp and moldy. Unlike oranges, mandarins do not keep well left on the tree, so the fridge is the way to store them.
seasoned: Refrigerated at about 32 to 36°F, mandarins hold two to four weeks. Store them loose or in a perforated bag so they do not sweat, and do not seal them airtight. Unlike a navel, a mandarin does not store well by leaving it on the tree, so the refrigerator, not the branch, is the place to hold the crop.

beginner: Whole mandarins do not freeze well, but the juice does. Squeeze the juice and freeze it in a sealed container for up to about six months. You can also freeze the zest for cooking.
seasoned: Whole mandarins do not freeze well, but the juice freezes excellently. Squeeze and freeze juice in airtight containers for up to about six months, and segments can be frozen in light syrup. Zest freezes for baking.

beginner: The big difference from an orange is that a mandarin does not keep well on the tree. Satsumas and most early mandarins should be picked as soon as they are ripe, because left on too long they get puffy and dry inside. Store them in the fridge instead. The exceptions are a few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie, which do hold on the tree into spring. Handle the thin-skinned fruit gently.
seasoned: The defining storage difference from a navel is that a mandarin does not hold well on the tree. Satsuma and most early mandarins should be picked promptly at maturity; left on the branch too long the fruit puffs, dries, and loses flavor. Refrigeration is the real storage method. The exceptions are the late holding types, notably Gold Nugget and Pixie, which do keep their quality on the tree for weeks into spring. Handle the thin-skinned fruit gently.

beginner: Mandarins come in many easy-peel, mostly seedless types that ripen from fall through spring depending on variety. Satsuma is the earliest and the toughest in cold. Clementine is the classic snack mandarin. Late types like Gold Nugget, Pixie, and Tango stretch the season into spring. Two things to know: many mandarins are seedless only if kept away from other citrus, and most tend to bear a big crop one year and a small one the next, which you can even out by thinning the heavy year.
seasoned: Mandarins (Citrus reticulata and its hybrids) span a long season by variety. Satsuma is the earliest and hardiest, ripening in fall to early winter; clementine follows in early winter; and late selections such as Gold Nugget, Pixie, and W. Murcott or Tango carry the season into spring. The two recurring themes across the group are seedlessness that can be undone by cross-pollination (isolate seedless types from pollen-bearing citrus) and a strong alternate-bearing tendency that is managed by thinning heavy crops. Satsuma and clementine also shrug off Alternaria brown spot that troubles tangelo and Murcott-type hybrids, a point in their favor in humid regions.

beginner: N/A for mandarins. Hardening off is for seedlings you start indoors, and you do not grow mandarins that way. You buy a young grafted tree from a nursery that is already used to being outdoors. If you move a potted tree into much stronger sun, ease it into full sun over a week or two so it does not sunburn, but that is just adjusting it.
seasoned: N/A. Hardening off applies to seedlings raised indoors, not to mandarins. Mandarins are bought as grafted nursery trees already acclimated to outdoor conditions, so there is no seedling-hardening step. A containerized tree moved to a much sunnier or hotter spot can be eased into full exposure over a week or two to avoid sunburn, but that is acclimation, not classic hardening off.

beginner: Buy a young grafted mandarin from a good nursery, certified disease-free, and in cold areas ask for one on trifoliate-orange rootstock for the best cold hardiness. Plant it a little high on a small mound with the knobby graft union above the soil. You can plant container-grown trees almost any time in frost-free areas; in colder areas plant in spring after hard freezes are past.
seasoned: Plant a grafted nursery tree from a reputable source with certified disease-free stock. In cold-edge regions choose one on a trifoliate-orange rootstock for maximum cold tolerance. Container-grown trees can be planted year-round in frost-free zones; in cold-winter areas plant in spring after hard-freeze danger passes. Set the tree at the same soil line as in the nursery container, high on a mound, and never bury the graft union.

beginner: Use a loose, fast-draining potting mix, ideally one labeled for citrus or cactus. Do not use heavy garden soil in a pot, since it packs down and stays soggy.
seasoned: Sharp drainage inside the pot is the priority. A mix sold for citrus or cactus works well, as does a quality potting mix lightened with extra perlite or coarse pine bark. Never use straight garden soil in a container because it packs tight and holds water against the roots.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Mix in perlite, pumice, or bark chips to help it drain even better. You want a mix that drains fast and never stays soggy, since a potted mandarin is even more sensitive to wet roots than one in the ground.
seasoned: Blend in perlite, pumice, or coarse bark to sharpen drainage. The goal is a mix that drains freely after watering and never stays saturated, since a potted citrus is even less forgiving of wet feet than one in the ground.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, especially in heat and wind, so check a potted mandarin often, maybe daily in summer. Water until it drips out the bottom, then let the top inch dry before watering again. Do not let the pot sit in a saucer full of water.
seasoned: Container trees dry out far faster than in-ground ones, especially in summer heat. Check the pot daily in hot or windy periods and water before the root zone dries out completely. seasoned: Water deeply and consistently through summer sizing. Uneven moisture over the fruit-development months shows up as splitting and pre-harvest drop, so a steady rhythm through the heat is the priority.

beginner: Taste a mandarin before picking, and once ripe do not leave it on the tree long. Most get puffy and dry if left on, so pick them and keep them in the fridge.
seasoned: Taste before you pick, then pick promptly. Mandarins color before full sweetness in some climates, and unlike a navel most do not hold on the tree: satsuma puffs and dries if left, so pick at maturity and refrigerate.

seasoned: For fruit that keeps on the tree into spring, grow a late holding type such as Gold Nugget or Pixie. These are the exception to the pick-promptly rule and store well on the branch.

seasoned: Keep pruning minimal on a bearing mandarin: deadwood, crossing limbs, and rootstock suckers from below the graft. Those suckers are the rootstock, often thorny trifoliate, and left to grow they sap vigor and can overrun the top.

beginner: Mandarin trees often make a big crop one year and a small one the next, which is normal. Steady feeding and watering plus thinning a heavy year help even it out, but a sudden big drop means something is wrong.

seasoned: A mature standard mandarin yields less than a full-size navel because the tree is smaller, commonly on the order of tens of pounds up to roughly a hundred or more pounds per year under good conditions, varying widely with variety, climate, tree size, and rootstock. Its defining advantage over other sweet citrus is cold hardiness: satsuma is the most cold-tolerant of the commonly grown citrus, with mature trees withstanding brief lows near 15 to 20°F, notably colder than a navel orange, which lets in-ground mandarins reach zone 8 across the Gulf South and interior valleys. Early ripening (satsuma from fall) also gets the crop off the tree before the hardest winter cold. Mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color and drop acid, so they are marginal only in the cool-night tropics and the coolest coasts. Two group traits shape their care: seedless types set seeds if cross-pollinated by other citrus, so isolation preserves seedlessness; and mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, managed by thinning heavy crops. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree and are picked promptly. Trees are small and grafted, usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness, and productive for decades.

beginner: Pick mandarins by taste, not just by color, and do not leave them on the tree too long. The skin loosens and colors as fall nights get cool, but in warm, humid areas it can still look a little green even when the fruit is ripe, so taste one first. Unlike oranges, most mandarins get puffy and dry inside if left on the tree, so pick them when ripe and keep them in the fridge. A few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie are the exception and do hold on the tree into spring. Early satsumas also let you pick the crop before the coldest weather.

The fruit then grows for about seven to ten months, a bit faster than an orange, so you harvest earlier: satsumas from fall, clementines in early winter, and late types like Gold Nugget, Pixie, and Tango stretching into spring.

beginner: Mandarins take cold better than any other common sweet citrus. A grown, hardened satsuma can handle a brief dip near 15 to 20°F without serious damage, colder than an orange (about 24 to 26°F) and beaten only by the kumquat. The fruit is more tender than the wood and can be hurt near 30°F, but satsumas ripen early enough that you usually pick before the worst cold. Because the tree is evergreen and never goes dormant, its leaves and wood can be hurt any time it gets cold enough, and young trees are the most tender. Planting on trifoliate-orange rootstock adds hardiness and is standard in cold areas. Mandarins also need less summer heat than an orange to get sweet, but they want cool fall nights to color up. The usual in-ground range is about zones 8 through 11.
seasoned: Mandarins are the most cold-hardy of the commonly grown sweet citrus. A mature, hardened satsuma withstands brief lows near 15 to 20°F without serious wood injury, notably colder than a navel orange (about 24 to 26°F) and behind only kumquat among edible citrus. The cold-hardiness order runs roughly satsuma and kumquat, then sour orange and tangerine, then sweet oranges such as navel, then grapefruit, lemon, and lime. The fruit is more tender than the wood, taking damage near 30°F for a couple of hours, but satsuma's early fall ripening usually gets the crop off before the hardest freezes. Trees are evergreen with no dormancy, so growing tissue is always vulnerable, and young trees are far more tender than mature ones. Trifoliate-orange rootstock adds cold hardiness and is standard for cold-edge planting. Beyond cold, mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color, so quality, not survival, is the limit in the warm-night tropics. The practical in-ground range is about zones 8 through 11.

beginner: Mandarins do not need any winter chill to flower or fruit. Unlike peaches and apples, which need hundreds of cold hours in winter to wake up and set a crop, citrus is evergreen and is triggered to bloom by spring warmth and moisture instead. So chill hours, which matter a lot for deciduous fruit trees, simply do not apply to mandarins.
seasoned: Mandarins require no winter chilling to flower or fruit. They are evergreen and do not enter a chill-triggered dormancy; flowering is driven by spring warming and moisture rather than release from a prior cold period. This distinguishes citrus from deciduous fruit trees such as peaches and apples, which need hundreds of chill hours to break bud dormancy and set a normal crop.

beginner: A mandarin makes fruit on its own, with no second tree and no bees needed, and most types are seedless when grown away from other citrus. Satsuma is naturally seedless. Clementine and some others are seedless by themselves, but if pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit ends up with seeds, so keeping a seedless mandarin away from other pollen-making citrus is what keeps it seedless.
seasoned: Most mandarins set a full crop on a single tree and are seedless when grown in isolation. Satsuma is parthenocarpic and reliably seedless. Clementine and W. Murcott are self-incompatible but facultatively parthenocarpic: they set seedless fruit on their own, yet fertile pollen from another nearby citrus cross-pollinates them and puts seeds into the fruit, and citrus pollen can travel a long way, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus is what keeps seedless types seedless. A few mandarin hybrids fruit better with a compatible pollinizer, but the common seedless mandarins need no pollinizer and no bees for a single tree to fruit.
